references.text: Jesus addressed the disciples after speaking to tax collectors and sinners. The context in Luke 15:1-2 shows that the parables in chapter 15 were directed at the Pharisees and scribes, while this parable about the dishonest manager is aimed at the disciples.

The term "manager" (οἰκονόμος) is also used in Luke 12:42, where Jesus asks who is the faithful and wise manager. Both passages deal with responsibility in managing what has been entrusted to someone.
The parable of the ten minas in Luke 19:11-13 also concerns the management of a rich man's possessions and being held accountable for how one has managed what was given into their care.
The parable of the talents in Matthew 25:14-15 has a similar theme: a rich man entrusts his property to servants, who are then held responsible for their management.
Jesus himself draws the conclusion from the parable in Luke 16:10-12, explaining that whoever is faithful in small things is also faithful in great ones – a principle of faithful stewardship.
1 Peter 4:10 urges believers to be good stewards (οἰκονόμοι) of God's varied grace and uses the same term for manager as in Luke 16:1.

Paul describes himself and his fellow workers as stewards (οἰκονόμους) of God's mysteries in 1 Corinthians 4:1-2, emphasizing that what is required of stewards is faithfulness – the same theme found in the parable.
In Isaiah 22:15-16, Shebna, who was steward over the king's house, is rebuked for his unfaithfulness – an Old Testament example of a manager who misused their position.
The expression "squander" (διασκορπίζων) possessions recalls the prodigal son who "squandered" (διεσκόρπισεν) his inheritance in Luke 15:13. The same Greek verb is used in both places.
The parable of the rich farmer in Luke 12:16-20 also concerns a certain rich man (ἄνθρωπός τις πλούσιος) who must give an account for his management of wealth.
